incidente.resumo: When a leap second set CLOCK_REALTIME back one second, clock_was_set() was not called, so the Linux hrtimer base.offset for CLOCK_REALTIME stayed one second ahead; TIMER_ABSTIME CLOCK_REALTIME timers expired one second early and sub-second ones returned immediately, causing load spikes in applications calling them in a loop. The state persists until clock_was_set() is called; the author proposes a fix calling clock_was_set when a leap second is applied. The text does not say how affected systems were restored.

gatilho.texto: A leap second occurs and CLOCK_REALTIME is set back one second.
trechos: Leap second occurs, CLOCK\_REALTIME is set back one second.

descricao.texto: Because clock_was_set() is not called when the leap second is applied, the hrtimer base.offset for CLOCK_REALTIME is not updated and the hrtimer code's sense of wall time is one second ahead of the timekeeping core's. At interrupt time the hrtimer code expires all CLOCK_REALTIME timers set up to one second ahead, so all TIMER_ABSTIME CLOCK_REALTIME timers expire one second early and all sub-second ones return immediately; such calls done in a loop (as commonly done with futex_wait or other timeouts) cause load spikes in those applications.
trechos: As clock\_was\_set() is not called, the hrtimer base.offset value for CLOCK\_REALTIME is not updated, thus its sense of wall time is one second ahead of the timekeeping core's.

At interrupt time (T), the hrtimer code expires all CLOCK\_REALTIME based timers set for T+1s and before, causing early expirations for timers between T and T+1s since the hrtimer code's sense of time is one second ahead.
This causes all TIMER\_ABSTIME CLOCK\_REALTIME timers to expire one second early.

More problematically, all sub-second TIMER\_ABSTIME CLOCK\_REALTIME timers will return immediately. If any such timer calls are done in a loop (as commonly done with futex\_wait or other timeouts), this will cause load spikes in those applications.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The faulty state persists until clock_was_set() is called (most easily done via settimeofday()).
trechos: This state persists until clock\_was\_set() is called (most easily done via settimeofday())

acoes.texto: Proposed fix (posted as an RFC potential fix): call clock_was_set when a leap second is applied; the author reports no longer seeing the issue with this fix.
trechos: With my fix to call clock\_was\_set when we apply a leapsecond, I no longer see the issue.
Re: \[PATCH 0/2\]\[RFC\] Potential fix for leapsecond caused futex issue (v2)

perguntas_em_aberto: Whether kernels older than v2.6.32.59 are affected has not been tested yet; the author is working to install an older distribution for further testing (others noted the bug has likely potentially been around since commit 746976a301ac in v2.6.22).
A to-do quoted from an earlier message remains: chase down the futex/hrtimer interaction to see whether the issue could be triggered in any other way.

observacoes: The document is a Linux kernel mailing list message (Sun, 01 Jul 2012) with a diagnosis and a test case; it does not state the date of the leap second or name affected services, so data_incidente is null and servicos_afetados is empty. status_relatorio is preliminar because the message presents an RFC 'potential fix' with further testing pending. The author reproduced the behaviour on kernel versions v3.5-rc4, v2.6.37 and v2.6.32.59. The hedged origin of the bug (commit 746976a in v2.6.22) is not treated as a causing change. status_relatorio is final: the post presents a diagnosis written after the leap second; the RFC and pending tests refer to the proposed patch, not to the report.
